GitHub offers Dependabot, an automated tool that can detect and even raise pull requests for
CVE by being configured to occasionally run against a repository (https://docs.github.com/
en/code-security/tutorials/secure-your-dependencies/dependabot-quickstart-
guide). CodeQL or Snyk and Dependabot are often seen used together. It's a common practice
to use multiple small and specialized tools in concert instead of one huge tool trying to do it all.
Whatever methods you decide to use, continuous scanning of the code base and your runtime
for CVE is critical. It's also important to make information about your code base available to
your cybersecurity team, your end users, and, if you have them, external customers, so that
they can understand their risk of exposure when a new security vulnerability is announced.
For this, you'll need to idx_ffe66c4e generate a software bill of materials (SBOM). The process of creating
an SBOM is newer, and the tooling around it is still imperfect. Open Clarity (https://
github.com/openclarity/openclarity) is designed to bring several of the best tools for
SBOM generation together to create as complete an SBOM picture as possible. It works for
cloud deployments and Kubernetes environments, making it a good option for ensuring that,
whatever your setup, you can have an SBOM.
However, AI implementations are different from the usual software implementation, and
tooling designed to satisfy idx_0d20f7c7 the SBOM requirements is not readily available. Fortunately,
OWASP idx_889cae1f has created an AIBOM generator, which idx_72c5b609 will generate an AI SBOM for models on
Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/spaces/GenAISecurityProject/OWASP-AIBOM-
Generator.
Let's take a look at an SBOM for Qwen/Qwen3.5-397B-A17B:
Figure 9.11: AIBOM tool

compliance purposes, but it also gives you a human-friendly view, which we'll show here:
Figure 9.12: AI SBOM

SBOM the JSON matches. It's important to know that this SBOM, which you can find in the

SPDX. Both idx_ac6010ef formats will provide important information with a great deal of overlap, but they
have different focuses. CycloneDX is the standard created by OWASP, and the primary
intention behind the design is to idx_9dcb9f16 make CVE identification easier.
SPDX was created by the Linux Foundation and places a stronger focus on surfacing licensing
information for the software supply chain within a project. Which type to use will be

Other best practices for zero trust
Unfortunately, we don't have idx_542503e9 the ability to go over every possible topic in this text. So, we'll
leave you with this list of other topics to consider for a zero-trust environment. OWASP
publishes a top 10 list of functional areas where security issues occur. This list is from 2021, as
the 2025 data is still being assessed and compiled for publication as of the time of writing:
A01:2021-Broken Access Control.
A02:2021-Cryptographic Failures
A03:2021-Injection
A04:2021-Insecure Design
A05:2021-Security Misconfiguration
A06:2021-Vulnerable and Outdated Components
A07:2021-Identification and Authentication Failures
A08:2021-Software and Data Integrity Failures
A09:2021-Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
A10:2021-Server-Side Request Forgery
The very first item, access control, is crucial. Access control is becoming the largest and most
critical area of security. With the idx_5516fcf6 ability to assign identities to software applications, managing
and revoking the permissions of these accesses becomes the most challenging aspect of
security to manage. You do not have to build from scratch here; as we discussed earlier, all
major cloud providers have solutions to accelerate your configurations. There are also many
third-party solutions such as AuthZed, Okta, and Keycloak.
Access isn't just about who can interact with which systems and what they're allowed to do,
but may also expand to dynamics such as where they can access from and how long they are
allowed to retain that access. Maximum session times and user location are common strategies
for maintaining both secure and compliant access.
You'll need to create access controls and policies for two types of user personas:
Human user access: Exactly as you'd expect, this is the access by human users to
software systems. For AIOps, this means ensuring that only users who should be able to
interact with production data and systems have access to prompting the AI model. This

access should be given only as needed; by default, it must be as restricted as access to a
production database would be.
Machine user access: If you want your AI to run agentically, it needs to interface with
other software. It will need an identity and a way to authenticate to the systems it must
investigate, and the systems that prompt it will need access to it in order to send the
prompts.
And the two of these shall not meet. If I have an identity with the same permission scope as an
AI assistant, our identities must still be unique. However, we could share a role or have distinct
roles with the same permissions for easy auditing. Once you've established the identities for
these personas, you must also establish what their scope of permissions is. For example, just
because I can interact with the AI doesn't mean I should be allowed to initiate an upgrade of
the server it runs on.
Some services, such as GitHub or even the Kong gateway we demonstrated earlier, will allow
unauthorized access to some aspects of the systems. When a user hits those public endpoints,
there's still a set of permissions for what they are and are not allowed to do. Functionally, the
system must assign them a temporary identity that maps to a specific role, and use that to
track and manage what the users do. What that identity is will be system-specific; it may be
the user agent, IP address, and so on. Exact implementations may vary, but there are still
permissions and policies for unauthenticated users just as there are for authenticated ones.
Identities and permissions must be paired with policies on the server side to ensure that there
are safety checks on all sides. A permission misconfiguration can be countered by a policy that
prevents dangerous actions, reducing the risk of human error introducing security gaps.
You may be astutely wondering whether permission and access reviews are an appropriate task
for an AI assistant. The short answer to that is yes. If you are using declarative systems such as
Kubernetes, where the RBAC configuration is all stored as YAML, then you can easily feed that
information from the source control into an AI assistant with the appropriate scope of
permissions to see it, and ask for a check of best practices. An easy check would be to see
whether there are any * (meaning all) permissions granted in any of the configurations, but
that can also easily be detected with automation. AI will be more easily able to identify cases
where there are conflicting permissions or permissions that could be improved.
A secure system is a trustworthy system, which is why we emphasized the importance of
governance and policies idx_17027e25 so early in the chapter. There are other relevant areas of security that
should also be evaluated against the OWASP Top 10, to ensure you've created the most secure

Data security posture management
Data security posture management (DSPM) centers data as the primary asset to secure in
cybersecurity. Data can be the idx_e68bff6b highest value asset you have, which is why it's critical to
properly secure and manage your data. AI makes vast amounts of data easier to analyze. Well-
indexed data is also faster and less idx_1c2d6395 computationally expensive to search, but just because it's
easy to keep data around doesn't make it a good practice. Don't get lazy about data lifecycle
management. With the security risks associated with AI still evolving, it's more important than
ever to use every trick possible to protect this asset. One key aspect of DSPM is the idx_3ff36cf2 use of data
discovery tooling. This is tooling designed to demonstrate where all data is created and stored,
and helps capture data that may not have otherwise been known to the IT organization.
In Chapter 5, we covered democratizing data, or making data widely available and actionable.
When data is democratized, it can be copied into various environments quite easily. This is
how production data often finds its way into test environments. It was for this reason that, in
that chapter, we touched briefly on the importance of securing your data and sanitizing data,
and what to do in the event of a leak. Data sanitization takes a few forms, all of which enable
the removal of any potential PII, but to differing degrees and in different ways. The AI gateways
we demonstrated earlier all have PII masking capabilities. As mentioned, ideally, log
sanitization, PII masking, credential salt, and hash are all handled at the application layer level.

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 338
chunks.content:
Chapter 9 338
The AI implementation also having these capabilities should be seen as a failsafe and does not
remove the need to adhere to best practices throughout the software stack.
In that segment, we advised removing identifying data in every way, so here we will contradict
ourselves a little. There are cases, however rare, where you might need to be able to identify
that all data belongs to the same user. When you do need to maintain the capability to
correlate all related data, token-based anonymization is an important practice.
Here, all PII is replaced with a token, which exposes no sensitive data, but can be indexed and
used for analysis if necessary. This could be useful for tracing a bad actor across a system
without compromising the security of everyone's PII. For example, if a user account is stolen
through phishing, your audit logs will have a history of what that account did while being
controlled by a bad actor, without the exact details of the account being revealed in the log
data. This allows all the critical information to be surfaced across systems and to users who
need access for the tracing, without the concern of access to PII. If you want to use AI to help
understand the scope of impact in the event of a security incident, tokens in audit logs could be
a helpful tool to ensure accuracy of the evaluation.
When data is tokenized, the PII it represents must still exist in a source of truth somewhere,
typically, via a relational database for when the data is necessary. This database must be
properly secured in accordance with the best practices, local laws, and regulations. However,
the benefit of having only idx_92697a2c one source of truth is that it offers the greatest reduction of risk you
can have.
In total, there are eight methods for data anonymization: randomization, generalization,
suppression, pseudonymization, tokenization, data swapping, data perturbation, and data
masking. In the case of observability data, they may or may not all be as relevant, and some of
the techniques, such as data swapping, could inadvertently create alerts in the wrong places if
not very carefully managed. Consider the approaches we've shown you throughout the
chapter, and mix and match them with additional approaches as you see fit.
Sanitizing your data is not enough; the next step is ensuring that you properly reduce or purge
old data. You can apply various techniques to do this, depending on the data.
For observability data, which is often in a time series format, a simple rule to delete data older
than a threshold will help to keep data storage down. This has multiple benefits, including
making the data you do have faster to search, lower costs for data storage, and an overall better
security posture. If you had a bug in your logs that exposed a password or key as plain text, the

chunks.heading: Chapter 9 338

faster you can roll those old logs off any storage systems, the better. A typical threshold for
operations data would be a 90-day retention. If you must keep data around longer than that,
we would recommend archiving it and identifying at what point you can delete that data. Data
you need available readily is at higher risk of exposure, so compressing data and moving it to
339 No Future Without Challenges
cold storage, where it's harder to get at, is a good best practice for any data that needs to stick
around a while without needing to be regularly searched.
It's reasonable that you may want to store some aggregation of the data in hot storage for the
purposes of charting historical trends, such as overall CPU and memory utilization trends over
the last year, or counts of how frequently customers interact with certain features. Data
sampling techniques can help you to keep your trend lines accurate without needing to keep all
the data around. You'll want to determine an ideal data interval and the means of calculating
the sampled data to keep. In Chapter 7, we covered how ACME Financial Services investigated
sampling and learned that there were multiple methods for this. For observability systems, you
will often be well served by taking random samples over the course of the target interval and
trending those. While sampling removes evidence of the spikes and valleys that would
otherwise appear if all the data were available, it keeps the same general trend line, which can
help you visualize things such as cloud spend or CPU utilization, month over month or year
over year.
While data security and the other idx_d53dc840 topics we've already outlined help to address the OWASP
Top 10, it's best to pair these with threat models for each area to ensure your cybersecurity
story is as complete as possible.
Threat models
Your threat model is a review of idx_b4722b6e your system architecture that helps you to assess what can go
wrong. According to the authors of the Threat Modeling Manifesto
(threatmodelingmanifesto.org), a threat idx_b2c14647 model should answer the following four questions:
What are we working on?
What can go wrong?
What are we going to do about it?
Did we do a good enough job?
Your system architecture will dictate how expansive the answers will be, as variables of your
decisions will greatly influence what can go wrong and what you can do about it. Additionally,
What are we working on? will almost always have multiple items in the What can go wrong?
follow-up, which will have multiple What are we going to do about it? answers as well. Let's
work through a miniature threat model together:
What are we working on?
Answer: We are working on an AI assistant for understanding our observability
data and making data-driven decisions on system scaling and health.

Chapter 9 342
As a relatively new frontier within idx_2377a683 software engineering, it's unsurprising that the idx_b1cb113f landscape
around cybersecurity and AI is full of unknowns and moving targets. As the technology
advances, best practices, security and compliance standards, as well as laws across localities,
are all playing catch-up. This space is rapidly developing and could look vastly different in a
very short period of time.
Mind the gap: How to maintain compliance when
implementing new AI technologies
You might notice that security and compliance are not lumped into one section, and this is
because they are not mutually inclusive topics. There is a Venn diagram between the two
topics; most certainly, SBOMs and threat models are excellent examples of common security
and compliance requirements. However, you can have a secure system that does not reach
certain compliance standards, and vice versa. Different industry verticals will have different
security and compliance requirements, so their journey may look different.
What is compliance?
Compliance is a checklist of idx_54f67bbf structured controls, policies, and procedures. Compliance
frameworks outline what those should be and are industry-dependent. As an example, the
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) is a medical compliance
framework in the idx_ce8dca02 United States that has very specific rules around how patient data is stored
and transmitted. There are security-focused compliance frameworks, such as ISO 27001, but
there are also legal compliance requirements, such as GDPR, that are geared specifically at data
privacy and include some security aspects as well.
While security can be deeply influenced by compliance requirements, they should never be the
sole motivation for having proper cybersecurity. You should also consider the compliance
framework as the floor of what is considered a secure system. They are by no means the ceiling.
Here are some of the most well-known compliance standards right now:

Although they may look similar on the surface due to some shared focus areas, each of these
standards has nuance and requires care to achieve the relevant certification of their governing
bodies. Notably, ISO has various certifications for which it oversees the compliance standards.
345 No Future Without Challenges
These don't just include cybersecurity, but many are still relevant to software engineers, such
as the ISO 26262, which is the idx_48fd5ef7 standard for automotive software.
In LLM-based AI, there are a few areas where you could find yourself running into compliance
or regulatory risks that didn't exist in previous generations of machine learning. The EU AI Act
is a perfect example of this. It's very broad and covers a variety of AI use cases. They provide a
nice exploratory tool to help you understand the new laws, which is worth a look regardless of
locale: https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/ai-act-explorer/.
Compliance risk 1: Data sources unknown
The amount of data that has gone idx_c4fda60c into training LLMs is more than can easily be conceived.
Unfortunately, this came with several notable examples of models being trained on data that
was not obtained legally. That hasn't had any impact on consumers of LLMs yet (https://
www.npr.org/2025/09/05/g-s1-87367/anthropic-authors-settlement-pirated-chatbot-
training-material), but it may present compliance concerns in the idx_c8810f54 future should laws
change.
Risk 2: Skills and MCP servers may not pass muster
While it is immediately tempting to leverage the skills and MCP server marketplaces, these
plugins for your AI model may not have idx_d999d64c been designed with the same legal and regulatory
compliance. Unless a skill or MCP server is totally secured from connecting to exterior sources
or limited to only well-known datasets, there's always a risk of compliance violation.
Risk 3: Data loss
Data loss is never great, but it doesn't always result in a compliance nightmare. However, some
industries need to retain records of the prompts and responses given to end users. For example,
think about a financial idx_46b7957c advisory AI app that gives you recommendations on how to invest your
savings. Those prompts and responses would need to be able to be stored and auditable. This
would allow you to demonstrate that you're abiding by various regulatory mandates such as
anti-money laundering, consumer protection laws, and United States Securities and
Exchange Commission (SEC) rules. If you're only relying on the LLM context window to keep

Risk 4: Bias in the AI
The only downside to data sampling and sanitization is that if that data is used for model
training or tuning, it can help introduce bias. This bias could lead to mistakes from the AI
agent. Bias can occur from tuning data idx_4a176854 and from within the current context. If the end user has
some bias, the AI will likely be swayed by that as well. This is known as availability bias. In
other idx_c6598690 words, the availability of data makes the assumptions seem statistically more likely. That
data existing, or the absence of any data to balance it out, can then reinforce the user bias.
Being mindful of bias during training and tuning phases for your model will be key to ensuring
that it's as impartial as possible. Just because we jokingly say, " It's always DNS," doesn't mean
we want the AI agent leaping to that conclusion in real scenarios. From a compliance
standpoint, a bias in training could cause an AI agent to take more destructive actions than
necessary, allowing it to become the reason for data loss or a credentials leak. Using model
accuracy evaluation tools can also help capture and surface bias.
Mitigations
Observability is part and parcel of compliance. If you've been following the recommendations
we've been making throughout the book, then you already know you can capture all those
prompts and responses and then idx_cf4285b8 extract and store them efficiently.
Policy, policy, policy. Your company policies, both written and technical, should enforce the
compliance standards to which your organization is subjected. You can make your AI aware of
policy through the use of instruction files, inclusion in prompts, and training. Use balanced
data during training to help ensure the safety of operations and keep bias to a minimum.
And finally, despite our hopes that idx_fe6c3c13 this book will help you be widely successful in your AIOps
implementation, don't forget about the humans. Human approvers may be required for
compliance, either legal or policy, and this still remains a best practice for now.
Summary
In summary, AI for observability and operations is a very promising area of the technical
landscape. There are problems that are not easily solved and involve large quantities of data.
This is the exact type of problem LLM-based AI was intended to solve, without everyone
needing to be a machine learning or data science expert.
But, as with any new technology, there are still some rough edges. It's important to be aware of
those and smooth them out during your implementation.
As we head into our final chapter, we'll look at ACME Financial Services and how they're
putting all of these learnings to use.

As we bring ACME Financial Services' journey to an end and set you off on your own path, we
will examine where we started and where we've ended up, and peer into our crystal ball to help
you anticipate what may come next. In this chapter, we will be covering the following topics:
What does building trust in AI look like?
What it means to be on the bleeding edge of AI before countries enforce regulations
The importance of securing the platform
Where your organization may differ from ours

Our story thus far
Before diving into the new directions that our fictitious company, ACME Financial Services,
might go, let's review the incredible journey the company has already undertaken. ACME
Financial Services, after having completed their cloud migration, discovered that their
observability practices were not sufficient or even adequate for their new cloud-native
architectures. They had a slew of problems to solve and formed an observability working group
to look into solutions. The initial proposal for tooling and training was accepted and
implemented. After the implementation, they realized that the improvements they had made
fell short of what was needed for the company to succeed. Costs didn't drop as much as they
expected, and senior leadership was not happy.
With their jobs being on the line and an unhappy senior leadership pushing for lower costs, the
observability working group reconvened with the goal of finding ways to reduce operational
costs, taking the following steps:
Determining what was driving the operational costs
Consulting their vendors on strategies to reduce those costs
Having discussions with the consumers of the observability tools
Along the way, they discovered new ways that the tooling could be used across the company to
reduce costs and positively impact multiple areas.
The result was a plan to implement sampling, as well as moving from policy-based data
standards to programmatically enforced data standards, which they hoped would lead to
immediate improvements. The outcome of this would be the increased utility of metrics and
decreased costs of running the observability tooling.
With the low-hanging fruit identified, they sought more ways to drive improvements and
return on investment. When they talked with the SREs and application developers who were
using the observability tools, they got divergent feedback. The observability working group

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera

chunks.content:
also discovered that they had originally looked at the observability problem through too small
a lens, which caused them to miss many opportunities for company-wide improvements and
maximizing tool utility.
It had become obvious that it was too difficult to coordinate the implementation of common
data across all the teams in the company. They would need a centralized control that would be
in charge of enforcing common observability standards.
The observability working group created another proposal for senior leadership that detailed
their idx_8bcccc48 findings and recommendations. Their proposal included an Internal Developer
Platform (IDP) with capabilities augmented by the agentic AI capabilities of their

observability vendor, along with details about the IDP and platform team. They idx_fee422ef pitched a
platform that enabled a new and scalable concept called self-service, a new utility idx_3418b6ce for the
observability tooling, including the new concept of business process observability, and plans
for cost management.
After a difficult series of conversations with senior leadership and several years of work to
implement the proposal, the original goals of the project were met and even exceeded. New
business intelligence, such as feature interaction metrics, created the framework for data-
driven product decisions. Company processes and procedures were reshaped in ways that the
working group hadn't foreseen, but ACME Financial Services came out of it much more
efficient and seeing lower overall costs.
Evolving trust in the observability platform
It took ACME Financial Services many years of effort to update the company's observability
practices and reshape the company around a new way of operating. Putting all the pieces in
place was just idx_f26a59f5 the beginning as that is what allowed the company to evolve within the new
paradigm. It was one thing to enable the use of a new tool and to provide data that was
previously unavailable, but quite another for the tools and data to become part of workflows.
Once workflows incorporated the new methods, it was yet another task for teams to start
trusting the feedback that the observability platform provided. It was not a quick process and
one that could not be rushed. ACME Financial Services cares deeply about its reputation with
customers, and trying to force the company to trust the observability platform was a difficult
task. Before any goals or mandates could be established, there would need to be a critical mass
of teams within the company that had modified their practices and showed tangible benefits.
These teams would be examples for others as the whole company transitioned their
workflows. Only once those examples and success stories existed could more stringent plans
be created.
This is not to say that senior leadership and the observability working group took a step back
once everything was in place. They aggressively pushed for consumption of the data and use of
the observability platform, while also stressing that teams would need to evolve their
practices. Senior leadership also pushed for OKRs to track company adoption of the
observability platform, with the goal of having 100% of the teams across the whole company
using it. They also created a KPI to track the accuracy of the suggestions made via the
platform's AI agent, and set an initial goal that the suggestions provided by the platform would
be correct 80% of the time. Their definition of accuracy was a suggestion from the

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 352
chunks.content:
observability platform that was accepted without modification. This was a very ambitious
goal, and everyone knew that such drastic changes take time and motivation, so those leading
the effort tried to motivate the teams and allow them to determine the timeframe.

The SREs' path to trust
It isn't surprising that the SRE teams were the first to incorporate the tooling and the first to
really trust idx_6c4b89e8 the suggestions from the tool. They were already very familiar with the type of data
produced by the observability platform, as well as already being heavily data-driven. In order
for the SREs to do their work, they had to rely on third-party-produced data and observability
tools. The SRE teams also introduced the observability working group to the concept of self-
service and recommended several ways to use ACME Observability more effectively. Extending
their workflows to incorporate suggestions from ACME Financial Services did not require
significant changes for the SRE teams.
However, even with the SRE teams rapidly adjusting to the new workflows, they did not trust
the suggestions they were given blindly. They were always aware that any mistake they made
could cause an incident, so they were very cautious about big changes by nature. They heavily
scrutinized every suggestion provided before approving it and allowing it to be accepted.
Whenever possible, they required changes be made in non-production environments first and
evaluated them. A series of metrics had been created to track KPIs on the observability
platform's correctness, but the SREs felt that that was too broad for their comfort level. They
needed something that would only track the correctness of the products they used. The
company-wide metrics had provided a blueprint for how to do this, so they created idx_ebcabe0e metrics
based on the company-wide ones but that were focused on their products. Then, they closely
monitored the metrics around the correctness of the suggestions that the observability
platform provided. When changes needed to be made to a suggestion by the observability
platform, they ensured that the tool knew about the changes and provided tweaks to help it in
the future.
Eventually, the recommendations from the tool started to regularly be 100% accurate and
didn't need any tweaks or modifications from the SREs. Being cautious by nature, the SRE
teams did not rush to automate acceptance of the observability platform suggestions. Instead,
they continued to monitor their correctness metric until they became confident that the tool
exhibited a sustained period of 100% correct suggestions. Once that milestone was reached,
the SRE teams started to allow the tool suggestions to be implemented without review and

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 352
chunks.content:
approval by the SREs themselves.
This was not the end of their trust journey, though. Allowing the suggestions from ACME
Observability to merge without review just created a new avenue for the SREs to monitor the
actions of the tool. The SREs created alerts to inform them whenever a change was
incorporated from the tool without their approval, and then created a process to review those
changes. If changes were made outside of normal business hours, then they were reviewed
early the next business day. As their trust in the tool's actions continued to grow, they slowly
reduced the frequency of their reviews. It went from every change to a daily review, to every

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 354
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 354
other day, to every week, and so on. Eventually, the reviews became so infrequent as to almost
not happen at all.
The developers' path to trust
Unlike the SREs, the application developers were much slower to adopt the new observability
platform. Engineers had a reputation for adopting new tools rather quickly when it made idx_8668add9 their
lives better, but in this instance, they didn't have a strong foundation in observability data,
which meant they had a difficult time understanding how it would benefit them. They were
also being asked to incorporate a new paradigm, observability-driven development, into their
design process, and they needed to understand what that meant in order to make the
requested changes.
Similar to the SREs, the application developers intended to start by heavily scrutinizing the
suggestions that came from the observability platform. This ended up being a little chaotic at
first, as some developers scrutinized the changes while others blindly accepted them without
understanding anything that was being done. Once an application team addressed that
inconsistency and got everyone to scrutinize the suggestions, they started to make progress.
The application developers reviewed suggestions from the observability platform for
correctness, as well as to understand the root cause that triggered the suggestion. The
application developers knew that they were going to need to incorporate observability-driven
development into their workflow, so they used the tool suggestions as a place to start learning
about what kind of data is needed and what kind of problems can be identified.
Once a suggestion from the observability platform was accepted, it was heavily tested in
development and preproduction environments before being deployed into production. This
meant creating testing scenarios that could create the issue that was being fixed and observing
that the change did in fact fix the problem. As the suggestions from the observability platform
continued to help alleviate production issues, the application developers started to trust them
more and also started to gain an understanding of how to design their applications to be
observed. This knowledge was critical for the application developers to successfully implement
observability-driven development.
With a basic understanding of the kinds of data that can prove useful to the observability
platform, the application developers began to change their design process to make it easier to
observe and understand the inner workings of their applications. At first, this was a slow
process, which is usual when implementing a new concept. As their experience grew and they
incorporated more observable designs, the quality and type of suggestions received by the
observability platform also improved. This increased the application developers' confidence in

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 354
chunks.content:
their new processes and the suggestions being provided. Making easily observable application
designs quickly became a self-reinforcing process change.

A trust framework was born
As various teams within ACME Financial Services charted a path to trusting the
recommendations idx_baa04344 from the observability platform, the observability working group
recognized similar patterns. They used those patterns to come up with a framework that teams
across the company could use to standardize growing trust in the platform's suggestions. They
broke the process into three phases: an experimentation phase, a trust phase, and a verification
phase. The framework was designed to be iterative, meaning that it could be used multiple
times to steadily build or improve trust as circumstances change. More aggressive targets, or
new and improved systems in the observability platform, could be reasons to go through the
process again.
The experimentation and dry-run phase
In this phase, the team gets used to interacting with the AI tool, in this case, the observability
idx_e25115e2 platform and its agentic capabilities, and learns what things it does well and where it needs
help. They can use tools such as DeepEval to help test and evaluate the results of their agentic
platform.
Also in this phase, benchmarks start to develop. They use natural language processing scoring
techniques to evaluate the correctness of the recommendations from the platform. To evaluate
the observability platform, the company recommends using ROUGE or BERT. Each team that
uses the observability platform will determine an appropriate score from the scoring system
that indicates their satisfaction with the suggestions. This will be the threshold that indicates
the solution is ready for use in production and against which future performance will be
measured.
Finally, they decide on a low-risk, high-value task to solve with an MVP and tune the responses
from the AI for that task. This should include consideration of what the team wants to do, how
they want to do it, and what access level is required by the AI.
By the end of this phase, the team should be receiving responses that meet the determined
score from the natural language processing scoring system. This indicates that the task is ready
to move into production, but not yet ready to trust and automate.
The trust phase
In this idx_3200490e phase, the team builds trust in the suggestions returned by the AI for the determined
task. They should be continually monitoring the responses from AI for accuracy and reliability.
They scrutinize any responses that do not meet the defined score threshold and decide
whether the suggestion is in fact correct or whether the AI knowledge or prompt needs to be

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 354
chunks.content:
tweaked. They continue testing with production data for as long as is necessary to trust that
the AI can automatically apply the suggestions without human interaction.

chunks.content:
Chapter 10 356
Once the team trusts the output from the AI, they should take on the task of automating the
application idx_c662dd08 of the suggestions. By the end of this phase, no one should be involved in reviewing
or approving suggestions from the AI for the defined task.
The verify phase
In this phase, human involvement for the specified task should start decreasing. Suggestions
from the idx_0da78d17 AI are being accepted and applied without human intervention, so human actions
revolve around monitoring and verifying the actions performed by the AI.
A key difference between the trust phase and the verify phase is that in the trust phase, each
suggestion is evaluated as it comes in, whereas in the verify phase, suggestions are evaluated
after they have been applied, as part of a regularly scheduled review. Observability tools take
over the task of monitoring whether the AI behaves as expected.
The frequency of the scheduled reviews would depend on the number of suggestions over a
period and the criticality of the task being performed. The team should pick a cadence that
they find acceptable and start there. As trust in the suggestions is reinforced through the
review process agreeing with the implemented suggestions from the AI, the time between
reviews can increase.
By the end of this phase, there should be little to no verification review processes required for
changes related to the specific task. The team is then ready to choose a new task and perform
the process again from the beginning.
How trust changed the company
It was one thing to tell teams in ACME Financial Services to do something, but quite another
for them to embrace it. In order to achieve the maximum benefit from ACME Observability, the
observability working group knew that teams would need to trust the suggestions provided
and eventually turn over responsibility for some things to the tool. Once the teams allowed the
tooling to be responsible for tasks in its domain, they would have more time to work on more
productive work for the company.
How SREs were impacted by trusting the tool
Once the idx_3d6aee6c SREs reached a point where they trusted the suggestions provided by ACME
Observability and allowed them to be implemented without review, their work started to
change rather drastically. All cluster and application scaling was handled by the observability
platform. Incidents from usage spikes all but completely disappeared. Incidents caused by an
application deployment were automatically addressed by rolling back to a previous version.
357 ACME Financial Services: How Will the AI Future Shape Our Company?
Incidents as a idx_df5801a9 whole dropped drastically. This benefited the SREs in two key ways:
The SREs didn't idx_3366e0ba have to spend as much time performing Root Cause Analyses (RCAs).

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 356
chunks.content:
Even with ACME Observability helping automate the RCA process, it was still time-
consuming for an SRE to put the data into a report and present it to leadership along
with what was done to prevent the issue from happening again.
With more of their time freed up, the SREs were able to focus on other tasks they
needed to perform. The implementation time for large efforts such as network
modernization and migration dropped as the SREs were able to devote more time
without interruption. This meant the SREs could improve and strengthen ACME
Financial Services' infrastructure much faster, such as adopting new best practices and
implementing better redundancy.
Perhaps contrary to what some might have expected, the total number of SREs needed within
ACME Financial Services didn't decrease. Large and old companies such as this have a long
history of legacy and outdated infrastructure implementations that need to be improved, but
the SREs rarely had time to tackle them unless a situation became critical. Even worse, many of
those legacy implementations were more costly or inefficient and had to be accepted idx_83e1f3c2 as the
cost of doing business. Many of them were so thorny, in fact, that no one wanted to touch them
even though they performed some critical function within the company. The people who had
originally created them had long since left the company, and the effort to understand and
modernize them was so large that the SREs just didn't have the time. It put ACME Financial
Services in a somewhat vulnerable position because it was far from certain that those systems
could be recreated if something failed or a change prevented them from operating. This risk
was not well understood by any of the decision-makers. Now, those legacy implementations
can be improved and ACME Financial Services has strengthened its resilience while also
reducing operating costs.
How developers were impacted by trusting the tool
As the idx_66821657 application developers gained trust in the suggestions provided by ACME Observability,
they began to be proactive instead of reactive. Instead of waiting for the tool to suggest
changes for things such as improving performance, handling an error case, or reducing
network congestion, the application developers started querying the tool for suggestions. Since
the observability data provided by their applications had improved, the tool was able to
understand what was occurring inside an application and provide useful suggestions to solve
problems before they occurred.
The quality of the applications improved measurably. They became more performant, more
resilient, and more secure. The observability tool was able to not only suggest changes based
on how the application was used but also automatically mitigate security vulnerabilities that

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 358
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 358
had been found in dependent packages. Updating dependencies to mitigate vulnerabilities was
always a time-consuming task that the application developers completely offloaded to the
observability platform.
With fewer idx_86eea1e1 bugs and performance issues, the application developers were able to concentrate
on creating value for the company. They were able to implement new features much faster
because they didn't have to spend significant portions of their time diagnosing and
determining fixes for production issues or working through dependency updates. They were
also able to work on long-desired application redesigns to bring their applications in line with
the company's various standards, such as authentication and trust, visual design, and log
formatting. This resulted in a more uniform look and feel and consistent function for the
company's customers.
Business process observability bears fruit
Implementing business process observability provided insight into the workings of the
company's idx_ddef1c42 applications and their interactions that the company never had before. They found
many failures in application interactions that led to less than expected resiliency, redundant
actions, and bottlenecks. Some insights that they gained after implementing business process
observability included the following:
Opening a new account involved multiple applications across several business areas.
Each performed its own authorization verification, and if any part of the process failed
or determined that authorization was not granted, then an error bubbled up and left
the process in an unknown state. Reattempting the creation wasn't guaranteed to
succeed.
Applications didn't share a trust model. Each application would verify authentication
and authorization independently, which created a bottleneck and resiliency concern in
their authentication system. This undermined the applications' design to ensure
resiliency through scaling their Pods.
They found many examples of a request ping-ponging across applications, for example,
A->B->C->A->B->D, because an application later in the request pipeline needed data
from an application earlier in the pipeline in order to make a decision.
With these kinds of insights, ACME Financial Services was able to improve their process flow
across most of their business operations. They ensured that no point in a process was a
bottleneck or limited the resiliency of their applications.
Incident idx_672c8964 response became much more efficient. Instead of bringing everyone into a call to
diagnose a problem, the incident response teams now knows exactly which applications are

application developers for issues that are not attributable to their application.
The importance of securing the observability
platform
ACME Financial Services were enjoying the multiple benefits that the new observability
platform provided. The observability platform had become so integral to the way the company
operated idx_e299af98 that it joined a small set of technologies deemed critical to the success of the
company. The fact that the observability platform can act on its own and has access to large
amounts of company data also added to the need to protect it with the strictest access controls
and other security mechanisms. They also had to make sure that the observability platform
doesn't violate any of the myriad regulations that govern areas of the company. Since the
observability platform acts upon large amounts of data, they have to constantly verify that
business or country regulations around strict access or storage of that data are being met.
That's in addition to the increased danger of having so much data available in one location.
Since the observability platform connects to so many systems, it has the potential to leak more
data than any previous system they have used. ACME Financial Services is no stranger to
securing sensitive data systems, and they have restricted access to the observability platform
in line with their most sensitive systems.
The company's more traditional data systems were secured using accepted procedures, but the
observability platform required additional thought and restrictions because of where the data
could be consumed. In most of their traditional systems, data was stored and then access to
that data was controlled such that no data could leave the company's network. ACME
Observability, like many of the newer observability tools, provides optional functionality by
connecting to the internet. This kind of functionality makes it very hard to control where the
company data is consumed, and that makes it incredibly dangerous. The observability working
group had to ensure that no data could leave the company's network, which meant all data had
to be stored and accessed only from within the company. That also meant that they could not
enable any functionality in ACME Observability that uses internet resources. Luckily, most of
that functionality was available to be installed locally, with the trade-off being increased
storage and compute needs for the tool and manual version upgrades. This was an acceptable
trade-off for ACME Financial Services and one they were familiar with, so they had plenty of
procedures to ensure the latest and most secure versions were being run.

Who can access the data
In addition to access and security controls for the systems, ACME Financial Services also had to
manage idx_42138e15 what data authorized people are allowed to see. One application team's data should
not be accessible by another application team. A financial advisor should not be able to see
client data for someone they are not advising. These kinds of controls are standard in ACME
Financial Services, but the new observability platform added another layer to the problem.
The company has always attempted to follow good security practices. Even with access to
source code repositories rigorously controlled, the company has strict policies that state that
sensitive data should not be stored in any source code repository. They treat supporting data
from a production system just like secrets or encryption keys. Since the observability platform
opens change requests in source code repositories, they had to be concerned with what data
the tool might attach to justify its suggestion. They made sure to configure ACME
Observability to provide links to itself rather than embed supporting data.
Managing the system
ACME Financial Services had come to trust the actions performed by their new observability
platform, but idx_30b795c5 that also created a larger burden around managing the platform itself. Since the
company had come to rely upon actions taken by the observability platform, it meant that
things such as version upgrades were incredibly tense and cautious affairs.
ACME Financial Services had ended up with a fairly common architecture:

This also idx_8101db67 meant that they had the same concerns with managing the system as many other
companies. A change to any component could have serious impacts on the functionality of the
system.
Any upgrade to the observability platform is undertaken with great care using a slow and
methodical process. Because the platform automates some functionality in response to
automated alerting, it means that any change caused by an upgrade could have serious
ramifications. It isn't enough to just look for functionality differences or to read over
changelogs. ACME Financial Services decided to incur the costs of running two versions of the
platform in order to perform upgrades. The current version of the platform will run and act as
it had been. A new complete stack with upgraded components will then run alongside the
current platform version, with access to all the same data and systems as the current platform
but it will not be allowed to make changes. The decisions and metrics of the new platform
version will be monitored and compared against the decisions and metrics of the current

chunks.heading: Chapter 10 360
chunks.content:
platform version.
If there is a deviation, then it will be scrutinized based on the type of deviation. If it produces
the same outcome but uses different reasoning to get there, then the reasoning is inspected to

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 362
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 362
verify that it is legitimate and reasonable. If the outcome is different, then that produces a very
involved analysis. Is the old outcome or the new outcome better? What data is used to make
the decision? Does the vendor have an explanation for why the newer version produces a
different result?
They will run both versions of the tools until there is confidence in the new version, then
switch over and allow it to actually do the work. They will keep the old system running a while
longer and continue to compare results until they are satisfied that the new version is running
properly. Only once they are completely confident in the new version will they tear down the
old version of the platform.
They also idx_f016b119 had to create a comprehensive set of actions and reasons for the decisions taken by
the observability platform. This was necessary to provide confidence in the decisions the tool is
making, but more importantly, it was required for regulatory compliance. The ability to
automate actions related to regulatory compliance would not be possible without the
necessary supporting documentation that the company could use during a regulatory
investigation.
Watch the drift
The new observability platform comes with a new area of concern. Since the observability
platform idx_35ec3c5f has become so integral to business operations, the company has to be concerned with
any outcome drift. Even with the tooling being isolated to just data within ACME Financial
Services, the observability platform could still consume data that could cause its effectiveness
to decline. They use dashboards and metrics to track the effectiveness of the decisions being
made by the observability platform. The detailed evaluation of decisions used for audits is also
conducted as part of the process to look for any drift in the platform's actions.
The continual efforts to stay current
Despite all the changes that have been implemented and the success that has come with them,
ACME idx_e96bab35 Financial Services can never allow themself to relax. They have always had to stay
current with changes in laws and regulations across the multiple regulated markets where they
provide services, but now they have to keep track of a whole lot more.
363 ACME Financial Services: How Will the AI Future Shape Our Company?
Monitoring industry trends
At the start of their journey, ACME Financial Services hadn't kept up with the changes in
observability idx_e6260ca0 practices and tooling, which led to them being in an unmanageable position once
they migrated to the cloud. They now know that they need to continually monitor changes in
observability practices, but they also have to keep track of security trends around observability
tooling. The new observability platform provides benefits across the company, but it would

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 362
chunks.content:
also be potentially catastrophic if that platform were compromised because it has access to so
much data and so many systems used by ACME Financial Services.
One of the most basic security guidelines the company has started to track is NIST guidelines.
They have made sure to stay up to date on the evolving recommendations and concerns for
securing their systems, workloads, and data stores. The FBI also publishes papers idx_aba1e62d and alerts
around cybercrime and security considerations, which need to be evaluated. Both NIST and the
FBI even have focus areas for AI, which is a core part of the observability platform that the
company has implemented.
Of course, they have to monitor industry changes in observability as well. They have stayed in
contact with the vendors of their observability tools and receive regular updates on changes in
the products, as well as where the vendors see things changing in the future. The company also
monitors project trends and discussions in open source projects such as OpenFeature and OTel.
It is an awful lot to keep track of, but not keeping on top of the rapid changes would mean even
more work later.
Expansion increases the effort
ACME Financial Services originally only served customers in the US, but with the increased
efficiency idx_9610490c enabled by the observability platform, they have expanded to additional countries.
This comes with increased and varying regulatory compliance. The regulations in the US are
complicated enough and regularly changing, but those regulations only cover the US. Europe
has a different set of regulations, and some of those require data to stay within Europe. In some
countries, there are multiple regulatory bodies to monitor for changes in order to stay
compliant.
Maintaining compliance with that many regulations and tracking regulatory changes is
daunting work. It would have been very costly and slowed new feature development
drastically if ACME Financial Services hadn't included regulatory compliance in their plans for
the new observability platform. The amount of work to track regulatory changes hasn't
decreased, but the cost of regulatory compliance has become manageable because the
observability platform is able to help developers and architects understand when violations
would occur.

Chapter 10 364
The cost of early adoption
Because of the timing of the problems at ACME Financial Services, the company has found
itself unexpectedly on the cutting edge of AI's impact on observability tools and practices. The
industry idx_f7a37e92 is far enough along that tools and new practices exist, but not so far along that
anything is known as the best or most cost-effective way to solve their problems. This alone
means the company has had to accept a larger degree of risk and accept that drastic changes
might be required should the industry shift in a new direction. But there is an even bigger
concern: governments.
All over the world, governments have been talking about regulating AI, and that is a core part
of the new observability platform. ACME Financial Services has had to monitor the discussions
and provide input whenever doing so would help the business use cases. A draconian or overly
restrictive regulation could jeopardize all the work they have already done. This isn't exactly
unfamiliar territory because they have already needed to track regulations across their various
businesses, but this is the first time they have been able to be involved in the discussions
around regulations. Usually, regulations change and the company has to react, so providing
feedback is not a position ACME Financial Services tends to find itself in. The company has
committed to helping shape regulations governing AI that would allow it to continue to benefit
from AI-powered observability tools.
Always monitoring the cost
ACME Financial Services has achieved such a level of success with the observability platform
that a new idx_8e169850 kind of cost concern has become paramount. At the beginning of the project, they
worried about the cost of running the platform and being able to show the benefit from that
expenditure. They now have metrics to show how the platform is positively affecting costs
across the entire company, but that doesn't mean that the cost of running the platform is
irrelevant.
As the observability platform becomes more popular, the number of requests to the platform
increases. As the requests increase, so do the processing resources required to perform the
requests and respond in a timely fashion. With the platform enabled to implement decisions
on its own, it isn't even necessarily company employees who are adding to the load on the
platform. The platform could actually end up straining itself with queries.
The cost for the resources to run the platform is to be constrained and monitored. The
observability working group will meet regularly to look over costs, types of queries, the source
of queries, and other cost-related data points and evaluate how the platform is performing. Are
the response times staying reasonable or increasing? Are the queries a good use of the

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 364
chunks.content:
platform? If they are not, the working group will contact the originators and ask them to stop
using the platform in a specific way.
365 ACME Financial Services: How Will the AI Future Shape Our Company?
Sometimes they will be able to optimize the cost by making queries more effective or tuning
the platform to better handle situations. Sometimes they will have to accept that more
resources idx_4b8e39ec are needed and scaling the platform is the correct solution. It is a never-ending
process to ensure that the costs of the platform do not spiral out of control.
Incorporating changes into roadmaps
Changes based on the various areas being tracked for changes have had to work their way into
company idx_2069db00 roadmaps. This isn't a foreign process because they have had to do it for regulatory
changes in the US, but the number of changes has increased and, at times, caused the re-
evaluation of priorities within some areas of the company.
Regulatory changes tend to come with a deadline for implementation. This is a process ACME
Financial Services is already well acquainted with; however, the number of changes required
increases with the expanded countries where they operate. With more changes and sometimes
conflicting deadlines, hard discussions have had to occur to ensure the company implements
changes for regulatory compliance by a host of deadlines.
They have also had to consider improvements and changes in security best practices or
changes to observability practices. This is a less familiar area for the company, and they have
had to learn how to manage planning these improvements while also allowing for new feature
development and regulatory compliance changes.
Application roadmap discussions have expanded from mostly new features, enhancements,
and bug fixes to include planning around a larger number of changes for regulatory
compliance. Platform roadmaps have had to expand to include more changes for regulatory
compliance, as well as including more frequent security improvements and application version
updates. With the volume of changes now required, it is impossible to prevent reducing the
velocity of new feature rollouts, but having discussions that are informed by upcoming
changes to regulations and best practices helps reduce the impact. Even with this reduced
velocity, they are still delivering functionality faster than they did at any time in the company's
history. The changes brought about by the observability platform have provided more capacity
with the same workforce.
The company has experienced some growing pains, but eventually, they have been able to
settle into a process that has allowed them to implement regulatory changes with enough time
to verify compliance before significant penalties could be assessed, and to improve their
software offerings as the primary objective, allowing application and security upgrades to have

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 364
chunks.content:
a longer horizon. They have discovered that this is a natural fit to manage timelines since
application upgrades and security enhancements need to move more slowly because of their
larger impact across the whole company.

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 366
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 366
So, what's next?
ACME Financial Services has been on a long and expansive improvement odyssey. What
started out as idx_ba7c8466 a need to update their observability practices after completing their cloud
migration has ended up reshaping the company in ways no one foresaw at the start. Their
journey has enabled the company to transition from very manual processes that consumed
large amounts of company time and productivity to streamlined automated processes and, in
some cases, complete hands-off operation. That is quite the cultural shift, especially in areas of
the business that are heavily regulated and therefore very nervous about change. It's fair to ask
where they should go next. What areas could be improved with their new observability
practices? As the observability industry continues to evolve, there is little doubt that there will
be new areas that can be improved.
Already on the horizon, there is work being done to improve security and threat detection
using observability tools. This would be especially interesting to ACME Financial Services.
Some of the markets they serve are very strict about interactions with embargoed or hostile
countries, and being able to proactively detect firewall misconfigurations or other exploits that
allow this kind of traffic would be an immense help in their regulatory compliance. That's on
top of basic improvements such as detecting security misconfigurations based on traffic
patterns or application behavior.
The observability working group's job is never really done. They will need to regularly evaluate
the effectiveness of the observability platform and ask a usual set of questions. Are teams
relying on it too much, or are they maximizing the platform's benefits for the team? Does a
benefit justify the potential cost or resource increase for the observability platform? Is there
anything new in the observability community that would make the platform better?
However, the observability working group knows that regardless of where the industry goes,
ACME Financial Services has done the kind of work that will enable them to adopt and benefit
from new directions and processes around observability.
367 ACME Financial Services: How Will the AI Future Shape Our Company?
Summary
The journey of our fictitious company is one designed to resonate with you, the reader, and we
hope it has achieved that goal. The work done by our imagined observability team is work
being done by operations experts industry-wide. We interviewed engineers and executive
leaders who all told similar stories of cloud transformations, exploding costs, and the struggle
to make something of the AI technological wave. By centering AI in an operational solution, it
moves from a solution in search of a problem to a solution to one of the hardest IT problems at

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 366
chunks.content:
hand. We've created this simple checklist to help you break down your AIOps project approach:
Define an outcome you seek to achieve through your AI implementation (OKR).
Start with one. You don't need more.
Evaluate tools and vendors to choose the technology stack you know you need now,
with exit criteria for what would lead to migration.
Use cost-benefit analysis frameworks to aid this decision-making process
Rank your AIOps use cases from the easiest implementation to the most difficult.
Use the crawl, walk, run approach to implement your use cases. Iterate to success.
Apply the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC): design, build, test, repeat.
Center security and observability at every stage
Measure your outcomes.
Define your KPIs.
Gather DORA DevOps and other performance metrics.
As technologies are advancing, the patterns for analysis, system design, and best practices that
we've outlined are intended to last even as some of the specifics may eventually become
obsolete. While the code we wrote may be gone in five years, if you can move forward with
those patterns and practices in mind, you'll be able to ride this and the next AI wave to success.
